cards.def: Chauncey Jerome was a New England clockmaker who used interchangeable brass parts to mass-produce inexpensive one-day clocks, then failed after a bad partnership and died poor, illustrating the market's boom-and-bust anxiety.

cards.term: Henry Clay, John C. Calhoun, and John Quincy Adams (as nationalists)
cards.def: Henry Clay, John C. Calhoun, and John Quincy Adams were the new nationalist generation that used federal power to promote development and dominated the Republican Party after the War of 1812.
James Monroe was the president who approved additional internal improvements as part of the New Nationalism after the War of 1812.
Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin and later contracted to mass-produce muskets with interchangeable parts.
Samuel Morse patented the telegraph, which knit the national market together with instant communication.
Robert Fulton built the Clermont, the steamboat that ran from New York City to Albany and pointed the way for steam on western rivers.
John Marshall was the chief justice who upheld private property and federal power in decisions that encouraged investment, competition, and corporations.
Samuel Slater was a British mill worker who slipped past an emigration ban and built the first textile mill in America.

cards.term: Francis Cabot Lowell and the Boston Associates
cards.def: Francis Cabot Lowell copied and improved the British power loom, and the wealthy Boston Associates then built the model mills at Lowell, Massachusetts.

Micajah Pratt was a Lynn, Massachusetts, shoemaker who hired workers in central shops, used standardized patterns and sole-cutting machines, and helped turn shoemaking from a craft into assembly-line work.
Sam Patch was a mill worker who made daring waterfall leaps, including a protest jump at Paterson, as a defiant display of a worker's "art" against machine labor.

cards.term: Mountain men (Jim Bridger, Jedediah Smith, James Walker)
cards.def: Jim Bridger, Jedediah Smith, and James Walker were far-western beaver trappers who worked as expectant capitalists for firms like Astor's American Fur Company, tying even the Rocky Mountain fur trade to the market.
John Jacob Astor organized the mountain fur trade through his American Fur Company and was one of the rare rich men who rose from the bottom.
Mary Paul and Sally Rice were New England farm daughters who went to the Lowell mills to earn their own money, a path most "mill girls" followed for only a few years before marriage.
